content.text: CSULB, following California State University system requirements, generally allows university bank accounts to be opened, changed, or closed only with authorization from designated campus financial officials, typically within the Division of Administration and Finance (Financial Management/University Treasury), rather than by individual departments or employees. Campus funds are expected to be deposited promptly into approved university depository accounts, and accounts must be held in the university's name, never an individual's. These accounts must follow CSU system standards (including the Integrated CSU Administrative Manual on cash management and banking) for internal controls, such as separation of duties, regular reconciliation, and restrictions on who may sign or transact. I'm not certain of the specific CSULB policy number, so you should check the CSULB Policy Office or Financial Management website for the current official text.

I can't recall the exact wording of that section of CSULB's Policy on Agency Accounts, so I can only describe how such provisions generally work. Agency accounts hold money that the university keeps as a custodian on behalf of another group, such as a student organization or an affiliated entity. The "prohibited use" section typically bars spending those funds on purposes that conflict with university policy, CSU system rules, or state law. Common examples are personal benefit or private loans, political contributions, and expenditures that would circumvent normal university procurement or personnel rules. For the authoritative list, check the current policy text on CSULB's Academic Senate or Financial Management website, or ask the university's Financial Management office.

I can't recall the exact wording of the "Internal Notifications" section of CSULB's Policy on Information Systems, so I can't quote or summarize it precisely. In CSU and CSULB information security policies, sections with this title typically require faculty, staff, and other users to promptly report suspected or confirmed security incidents, such as unauthorized access, lost devices, or breaches of protected data, to the campus Information Security Officer or the IT Service Desk. Those offices then escalate the incident internally to appropriate administrators, data owners, and possibly the CSU Chancellor's Office. They may also decide whether external notification is legally required, for example under California's breach notification law. For the authoritative text, check the CSULB Policy website or contact the campus Information Security Office.

CSULB's catalog makes students responsible for knowing and following the university's academic regulations, degree requirements, policies, and published deadlines, such as those for adding or dropping classes, withdrawal, and graduation. Lack of awareness is generally not accepted as grounds for an exception, and advice from faculty or staff does not override published requirements. Students are also expected to monitor their official CSULB email and MyCSULB accounts, keep their records current, and follow each course syllabus. Student conduct, including academic integrity, falls under the CSU Student Conduct Code (Title 5, California Code of Regulations, Section 41301). For the exact wording, check the current CSULB Catalog or ask the Office of Enrollment Services or Student Conduct and Ethical Development, and let me know if you meant a specific aspect of student responsibility.

Under CSULB's policy on the appointment and review of department chairs, the chair serves at the pleasure of the President, so the President, typically acting on the dean's recommendation, holds the final authority to remove a chair before the term ends. As I recall, removal can be initiated either by the dean or by a petition from the department's faculty. The dean is then expected to consult with the department faculty, which may include a vote of confidence, before making a recommendation. I'm not certain of the specific thresholds, such as the share of faculty needed to trigger a review, or of the current policy number, so check the official CSULB Academic Senate policy for those details.

At CSULB, "complainant" is defined mainly under the CSU systemwide nondiscrimination policy, which replaced the earlier Executive Orders 1096 and 1097. Under that policy, a complainant is a student, employee, or third party who is alleged to have experienced discrimination, harassment, sexual misconduct, dating or domestic violence, stalking, or retaliation. Complaints are handled through the campus Title IX and Equity office. The complainant is entitled to supportive measures, protection from retaliation, an advisor of their choice, timely written notice of the process and outcome, and the right to appeal. Complainants may also choose whether to participate in an investigation, and the university limits disclosure of their information to what is needed to respond.

At CSULB, staff positions are generally expected to have a current, written position description that outlines the job's purpose, essential duties, the approximate percentage of time spent on each, required qualifications, and reporting relationships. The supervisor or department typically drafts or updates it, and Human Resources (Classification and Compensation) reviews it to place the position in the appropriate CSU classification and skill level under the system's classification standards and the applicable collective bargaining agreement. Position descriptions are usually reviewed and updated when duties change significantly, often alongside the performance evaluation cycle, and employees should receive a copy. Substantial changes in duties can be grounds for a reclassification review. I'm not certain of a specific CSULB policy number for this, so for exact procedures and forms you should check with CSULB Human Resources or your bargaining unit's contract.

I can't confirm the exact wording or policy number of a CSULB policy titled "criminal penalties for fraud and abuse." In general, CSULB, following CSU systemwide rules, holds that fraud, theft, misuse of university resources, and unauthorized or abusive use of computing systems can lead to university discipline and criminal prosecution. Such conduct may be referred to University Police and prosecuted under laws such as the federal Computer Fraud and Abuse Act and California Penal Code Section 502, with possible fines, restitution, or imprisonment. Suspected fraud or abuse can also be reported through the CSU whistleblower process. For the authoritative text, check CSULB's official policy pages or the Office of Internal Audit and Advisory Services.

I'm not certain of the exact wording or number of a CSULB policy devoted specifically to event set-up, so I can only describe how it generally works on campus. Set-up needs such as tables, chairs, staging, and audiovisual equipment are typically requested through the campus space-reservation process when the event is booked, and the unit that manages the venue (for example, University Student Union event services or the campus facilities and events offices) does the work, often with an advance-notice deadline and possible labor or equipment charges. Organizers are generally expected to follow fire-code occupancy limits and safety rules and to avoid altering facilities on their own. For the authoritative and current requirements, check CSULB's official policy site or contact the office that manages the specific venue.

I can't point to the exact text or a policy number for a CSULB credit card policy, and "credit cards" could refer to several different university rules. If you mean the university-issued Procurement Card (ProCard), CSULB generally limits its use to authorized business purchases within set spending limits, prohibits personal use, and requires cardholders to keep receipts and reconcile statements on schedule. If you mean accepting credit card payments for a department or event, campus units typically must get approval through the university's financial offices and comply with Payment Card Industry (PCI) data security standards. Since I'm not sure of the current details, check with CSULB Financial Management or Procurement Services, or tell me which situation you're asking about.

I don't have reliable knowledge of a CSULB "Policy on Student Organization Grants" or the specific wording of a "Use of Grant Funds" section, so I can't accurately explain what it requires. Sections with that title in university grant policies typically limit spending to the purposes approved in the application, list prohibited expenses (such as alcohol, personal gifts, or items for individual benefit), and require receipts or a post-event report. Whether CSULB's policy says any of this, I can't confirm. For the authoritative text, check with CSULB's Student Life & Development office, Associated Students, Inc. (ASI), or the university's official policy website.

I can't recall the exact wording of CSULB's Regulation XIII, so I can only describe what this kind of provision typically means. Disclosure sections like this usually rest on the federal Family Educational Rights and Privacy Act (FERPA), as amended by the Higher Education Amendments of 1998. That amendment lets a university notify the parents or legal guardians of a student under 21 when the student is found to have violated federal, state, or local law, or campus policy, on the use or possession of alcohol or controlled substances. Such notification is generally at the university's discretion rather than required. Check the current CSULB catalog or the Office of Student Conduct and Ethical Development for the precise terms CSULB applies.

CSULB's policy on the appointment and review of department chairs allows a department, where its size or complexity justifies it, to have one or more associate chairs who help the chair with administrative duties. As I understand it, the chair typically recommends the associate chair after consulting the department faculty, and the college dean makes the appointment. The associate chair's duties, term, and any assigned time or compensation are usually set by the chair and dean, and the associate chair generally serves in support of, and at the discretion of, the chair. I'm not certain of the policy number or the exact wording, so please check the current text in CSULB's Academic Senate policy library.

I don't have reliable knowledge of the specific direct payment procedures in CSULB's Policy on Accounting, so I can't describe its exact provisions or cite a policy number. At CSU campuses generally, direct payments are a way to pay certain approved categories of expenses, such as honoraria, memberships, subscriptions, registration fees, or reimbursements, without a purchase order. Such requests typically require a completed payment request form, supporting documentation like an invoice or receipt, and authorization by an appropriate budget approver before Accounts Payable processes them. For the authoritative procedures, check the CSULB Financial Management or Accounts Payable website, or the campus policy repository.

I'm not certain of the exact wording, so please treat this as a general recollection rather than an authoritative quote. My understanding is that CSULB's Policy on Agency Accounts treats revenue generated through activities or programs funded with Associated Students (ASI) fees differently from money a campus group raises independently. Such revenue is generally expected to return to, or remain under the control of, the Associated Students rather than being deposited into a separate agency account for the group's own discretionary use. Because I can't confirm the policy number or the precise provision, check the current text with CSULB's Academic Senate policy archive, Associated Students, Inc., or University Financial Services.

I can't recall the exact wording of CSULB's Policy on Facilities Use on this point, so I can't give you the precise language or policy number. Generally, CSU campuses, CSULB likely among them, distinguish commercial filming, which requires a permit, fees, and insurance, from non-commercial filming such as class projects, academic work, or personal photography. Non-commercial filming is usually allowed with fewer formalities as long as it doesn't disrupt university operations, block walkways or building access, or invade others' privacy. Larger shoots that use substantial equipment or crews, reserve or close spaces, or take place inside restricted facilities may still need advance approval through the campus office that handles facility reservations or filming. For the authoritative rules, check the current policy on CSULB's website or contact the office that handles campus filming.

At CSULB, complaints of discrimination, harassment (including sexual harassment and sexual misconduct), and retaliation are generally handled under the CSU systemwide Nondiscrimination Policy and its procedures, which replaced Executive Orders 1096 and 1097. Campus offices such as the Title IX and equity office receive these complaints and investigate them. The process typically includes an intake review and notice to the parties, and both sides get the chance to present evidence and witnesses. An impartial investigator then applies a preponderance of the evidence standard and issues a written outcome, which the parties can usually appeal to the CSU Chancellor's Office. Timelines and procedures differ depending on whether the respondent is a student, employee, or third party, so check the current policy text or contact the campus equity office for the details that apply to your situation.

I can't recall the specific wording of CSULB's Hazard Communication Program, so this reflects how such programs are typically structured under Cal/OSHA's Hazard Communication standard (Title 8, Section 5194), which the CSULB program implements. In that framework, engineering controls are the preferred, first-line way to reduce employee exposure to hazardous chemicals. They include local exhaust ventilation and laboratory fume hoods, enclosure or isolation of processes, and substitution of less hazardous materials. These controls are generally favored over administrative controls and personal protective equipment in the hierarchy of controls. Departments are typically responsible for making sure the controls are used and maintained, for example through regular fume hood inspections coordinated with Environmental Health and Safety. For CSULB's exact language and responsibilities, check the program document published by CSULB's Environmental Health and Safety office.

At CSULB, "initiation" falls under hazing rules, which prohibit any method of initiation or pre-initiation into a student organization that causes or is likely to cause bodily danger, physical harm, or serious psychological or emotional harm to a student or other person. This applies to all affiliated organizations, including fraternities, sororities, clubs, and athletic teams. The prohibition comes from the CSU Student Conduct Code (Title 5, California Code of Regulations, Section 41301) and California Penal Code Section 245.6 ("Matt's Law"). Neither the victim's consent nor the activity happening off campus is a valid defense. Violations can lead to student discipline up to expulsion, loss of recognition for the organization, and possible criminal charges, so check CSULB's Student Conduct and Ethical Development office for the current campus-specific procedures.

I don't have reliable knowledge of the exact wording of the CSULB Associated Students, Inc. (ASI) Bylaws for 2025-26, so I can't quote what they say about installing officers. Generally, ASI bylaws provide that newly elected officers, such as the ASI President, Vice President, and Senators, are installed and take an oath of office at a designated point near the end of the spring semester or the start of the new fiscal year, often at a transition meeting of the Senate. For the precise timing, oath requirements, and procedures, check the current bylaws posted on the ASI website (asicsulb.org) or contact the ASI Government office.

CSULB follows the federal Jeanne Clery Disclosure of Campus Security Policy and Campus Crime Statistics Act (the Clery Act) for records of on-campus crime. The University Police Department keeps a daily crime log of reported crimes on campus and nearby property, and the public can inspect it during normal business hours. CSULB also publishes an Annual Security and Fire Safety Report each year by October 1, with three years of crime statistics and the university's security policies, and makes it available to current and prospective students and employees. California law, including the Kristin Smart Campus Safety Act, also governs how the campus documents and reports certain crimes, and CSU systemwide policies guide these practices.

I'm not aware of a single CSULB document titled "general policies," so the question may be referring to how the university creates and manages its policies in general. At CSULB, academic policies are typically developed through the Academic Senate, approved by the President, and issued as numbered Policy Statements. Administrative policies come from the relevant administrative divisions, and all campus policies must be consistent with California State University (CSU) system policies and Title 5 of the California Code of Regulations. Because I can't confirm a specific policy number or its exact provisions, please check the CSULB Academic Senate's policy statements page or the university's official policy library for the current, authoritative text.

At CSULB, discrimination, harassment, and retaliation complaints fall under the CSU systemwide Nondiscrimination Policy and its procedures, which the campus implements through its Office of Equity & Diversity (the DHR Administrator and Title IX Coordinator). As I understand it, early resolution is an informal, voluntary alternative to a formal investigation. It can usually be initiated after intake, either because the complainant requests it or because the DHR Administrator or Title IX Coordinator offers it when it seems appropriate. It generally requires the complainant's agreement, and the administrator may decline it when the allegations are serious or there is ongoing risk to the campus community. Outcomes can include facilitated conversations, education or training, or other remedial measures, and the matter can move to a formal investigation if early resolution fails. Check the current policy text for exact eligibility rules and timelines, since the procedures have been revised several times.

At CSULB, the reappointment, tenure, and promotion (RTP) process follows a calendar that Academic Affairs (Faculty Affairs) publishes each academic year. It sets deadlines for candidates to submit their files, typically early in the fall semester, and for each level of review to complete its evaluation, generally the department committee, department chair, college committee, dean, and finally the Provost/President. Under the CSU–CFA collective bargaining agreement (Article 15), candidates must receive a copy of each level's written recommendation and have 10 days to submit a rebuttal or response, or request a meeting, before the file moves on. Probationary faculty normally serve a six-year probationary period with periodic reviews, and requests for early tenure or promotion follow the same calendar. For exact dates in a given year, check the current university RTP policy and the annual RTP calendar from Faculty Affairs, along with any college- and department-level RTP documents.

I can't recall the exact wording of the "Special Meetings" provision in the CSULB Academic Senate Bylaws, so I can only describe how such sections typically work. Generally, a special meeting is one held outside the regular schedule. It can usually be called by the Senate Chair or the Executive Committee, or by a written petition from a specified share of the members. Notice must normally be given in advance and state the purpose, and business is often limited to the items in the call. For the exact rules on who may call a meeting, required notice, and quorum, check the current Bylaws on the CSULB Academic Senate website or contact the Senate office.

I can't confirm the exact text of CSULB's Title IX Resources Handbook. A "W Broadway, Long Beach, CA 90802" address in a list of Title IX resources most likely refers to the Long Beach Police Department headquarters at 400 W. Broadway, an off-campus law enforcement option for reporting sexual misconduct. Such handbooks typically note that you can file a criminal report with local police, with University Police, or both, and that this is separate from, and can happen alongside, a report to the campus Title IX Office under the CSU's systemwide nondiscrimination policy. For the exact listing and current contact details, check the handbook itself or contact CSULB's Title IX Office directly.

The Age Discrimination Act of 1975 is a federal law that prohibits discrimination based on age in programs and activities that receive federal financial assistance, which includes universities like CSULB. At CSULB, age is a protected status under the CSU systemwide Nondiscrimination Policy (which replaced the former Executive Orders 1096 and 1097). Under that policy, students, employees, and applicants may not be denied participation in, denied the benefits of, or subjected to discrimination in university programs and activities because of their age, though the law allows certain narrow exceptions, such as age distinctions required by law or necessary to a program's normal operation. Complaints of age discrimination at CSULB are generally handled through the campus Office of Equity and Compliance (sometimes listed as the Office of Equity and Diversity), and you should check with that office or its website for the current procedures and contacts.

I don't know the exact wording of the 2025-26 CSULB Associated Students, Inc. (ASI) Bylaws on length of term of office, so I can't quote or cite that section reliably. Generally, ASI elected officers at CSULB, such as the President, Vice President, and Senators, serve one-year terms tied to the academic or fiscal year, typically running from around June 1 through May 31 after spring elections. The bylaws also usually address mid-term vacancies, appointments to fill unexpired terms, and any limits on how many terms one person may serve. For the authoritative text, check the current ASI Bylaws on the ASI website (asicsulb.org) or contact the ASI Government office.

CSULB's Policy on Master's Degrees includes a section on academic load that defines what counts as a full-time course load for graduate students and limits how many units a student may take in a semester without special approval. My understanding is that it ties full-time status to a set number of graduate-level units per semester. It also requires students who want to exceed the normal maximum to get approval, typically from their graduate advisor or college. I'm not confident about the exact unit thresholds or the policy number. Please check the current policy text on CSULB's Academic Senate policy site or the graduate section of the University Catalog, especially if your financial aid, visa status, or assistantship depends on the load definition.

I can't recall the exact wording of the "Improper Transactions" section of CSULB's Policy on Signature Authorization, so I can only describe what such sections typically cover. In university signature-authority policies, this part usually says that anyone who signs or approves a transaction without proper delegated authority, or beyond the limits of that authority, has acted improperly. The university may decline to honor such a commitment, and the individual may be held personally responsible for the obligation. Such sections also typically warn that knowingly making unauthorized commitments can lead to disciplinary action, and that authority cannot be sidestepped by splitting a transaction into smaller pieces to stay under approval limits. For the authoritative language, check the current policy on CSULB's official policy website or contact the Office of Financial Management or University Controller.

As far as I know, CSULB's Repetition of Courses policy does not address college RTP (Retention, Tenure, and Promotion) policy at all. It is an academic policy governing students, covering when undergraduates may repeat a course, the limits on grade forgiveness and repeated units, and how repeated grades are calculated in the GPA. RTP is a separate faculty personnel matter, handled under the university's RTP policy and the college- and department-level RTP documents that implement it. If you saw a reference linking the two, check the current CSULB Academic Senate policy listings or the Office of Faculty Affairs to confirm.

I don't know the exact wording of the "User Access" section of CSULB's Policy on Information Systems, so I can't reliably summarize it. Generally, user access provisions in CSU campus policies, which align with the CSU systemwide Information Security Policy and its access control standards in the ICSUAM 8000 series, say that access to university systems and data is granted on a least-privilege, need-to-know basis tied to a person's job role. They typically make users responsible for protecting their credentials and require that access be reviewed periodically and promptly revoked when a person's role changes or they leave the university. For the authoritative text, check CSULB's official policy site or contact the campus Information Security Office.

I can't recall the exact wording of CSULB's policy on Extension programs, so this reflects the general CSU framework rather than the specific text. Extension and self-support programs, now run through the College of Professional and Continuing Education, may use campus facilities such as classrooms, labs, and equipment. However, state-supported instruction and regular campus activities generally get priority, so Extension uses space when it is available and doesn't displace state-funded programs. Because Extension is self-supporting, it is typically expected to pay the campus for its use of facilities and services rather than having state funds subsidize it. Please check the current policy on CSULB's Academic Senate or policy website for the precise provisions and policy number.

CSULB's policy on participation in the legislative process generally separates acting as a private citizen from speaking on behalf of the university. Faculty, staff, and students may contact legislators, testify, or take positions on legislation as individuals, but they should make clear they are not representing CSULB and should not use university time, letterhead, or other state resources for personal advocacy. Official university positions on legislation are coordinated through the President's office and the campus government relations function, consistent with the CSU Chancellor's Office, which sets system-wide legislative positions. I'm not certain of the exact policy number or current wording, so check the CSULB Academic Senate policy statements or the Office of Government Relations for the authoritative text.

I don't have reliable knowledge of the exact wording of the "Volunteer Recruitment and Selection" section of CSULB's Policy on Volunteers, so I can't quote it or give its policy number with confidence. In general, sections like this at CSU campuses say that the department using a volunteer is responsible for recruiting and screening them. That usually means defining the volunteer's duties in writing, making sure the role doesn't displace paid employees, and having the volunteer complete a campus registration or agreement form before starting. Departments are also typically expected to apply background checks or other screening when the role involves minors, sensitive data, or security-sensitive duties, consistent with CSU systemwide rules. For the precise requirements, check the current policy on CSULB's Policies and Procedures website or ask CSULB Human Resources or Risk Management.

"SRWC - Bldgmnt" most likely refers to building management at CSULB's Student Recreation and Wellness Center (SRWC), where student building managers and facility staff enforce the facility's conduct and usage rules. Generally, you must present a valid CSULB ID or SRWC membership card to enter, wear appropriate athletic attire and closed-toe shoes in activity areas, and limit drinks to water in closed containers outside designated eating areas. Patrons are expected to follow staff instructions, re-rack equipment, use day-use lockers only during their visit, refrain from unauthorized personal training, and report injuries or hazards right away. Violations can result in being asked to leave or losing facility privileges. Because I don't know the exact current policy text, check the SRWC website or ask staff at the front desk for the official, up-to-date rules.

I don't know the specific text of a CSULB document called "Regulation X," so I can't reliably say what it states about information tables. Generally, CSULB's campus rules on time, place, and manner of expression allow registered student organizations and other permitted groups to set up information tables in designated outdoor areas. Typical conditions include reserving the space in advance, staying within assigned locations and hours, not blocking walkways or building entrances, and following rules on amplified sound and distributing literature. For the exact wording, check the current CSULB policy statements or contact the Office of Student Life and Development.

"Program structure" can refer to several different CSULB policies, so the answer depends on which one you mean. Generally, CSULB degree programs follow CSU system rules. California Code of Regulations Title 5 sets a minimum of 120 semester units for most bachelor's degrees and 30 units for master's degrees. CSU Executive Order 1071 defines how majors can be organized into subprograms such as concentrations, options, and minors, including minimum unit and overlap expectations. CSULB's Academic Senate policies add campus-level rules on creating and revising programs and on general education. If you tell me which aspect you need, such as unit limits, concentrations, minors, or certificates, I can be more specific. You should confirm the current details in the CSULB Catalog or with the Academic Senate office.

I can't quote CSULB's exact policy language or number with confidence, so treat this as general guidance. CSULB, like other CSU campuses, follows systemwide rules (Title 5 and CSU Chancellor's Office directives) that set most bachelor's degrees at 120 total units. Campus policy then limits how many of those units a major may require, so students have room for General Education and electives. Majors that need more units, often for accreditation or licensure, usually must get special approval. For the current unit caps and any exceptions, check the CSULB Academic Senate policy statements on baccalaureate degree requirements or the University Catalog, or ask your college advising center.

I'm not confident of the exact wording of the "Kiosks" section of CSULB's Time, Place and Manner policy, so I can only describe it in general terms. As I understand it, the kiosks are freestanding posting structures on campus designated for flyers and notices, and they are generally open to campus community members and, in some cases, outside parties as a forum for expression. Such policies typically regulate only content-neutral matters, such as size limits, how materials may be attached, how long items may stay up, and periodic clearing of the kiosks. They also usually prohibit covering other people's postings and limit posting to the kiosks rather than nearby walls, trees, or buildings. For the precise rules, check the current policy on CSULB's website or contact the Division of Student Affairs.

CSULB holds a Federalwide Assurance (FWA) with the Office for Human Research Protections (OHRP) in the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services. Through it, the university commits that all human subjects research conducted under its auspices will follow the ethical principles of the Belmont Report and the federal regulations at 45 CFR 46 (the Common Rule), regardless of funding source. Research involving human participants must be reviewed and approved, or determined exempt, by CSULB's Institutional Review Board (IRB) before it begins. Investigators must obtain and document informed consent as required, complete required human subjects training, report unanticipated problems and noncompliance, and submit modifications for IRB approval before implementing them. The Office of Research and Sponsored Programs (ORSP) oversees compliance, maintains the FWA, and can suspend or terminate research that does not meet these requirements, but I'm not certain of the specific CSULB policy number.

At CSULB, reassigned time and Faculty Small Grant awards are part of the university's internally funded Research, Scholarly and Creative Activity (RSCA) program, which the Office of Research and Sponsored Programs (ORSP) coordinates and the individual colleges administer. Awards are generally competitive and reserved for tenured and tenure-track faculty. Applications are typically reviewed by college-level committees against published criteria such as scholarly merit, feasibility, and the likelihood of producing publications, creative work, or external grant proposals. Reassigned time usually takes the form of course release, often three units for a semester, while small grants fund expenses such as supplies, travel, or student assistants, and recipients are generally expected to submit a final report on outcomes. I'm not certain of the current dollar caps, deadlines, or any limits on holding both awards at once, so check the current ORSP call for proposals and your college's guidelines for the governing details.

I'm not certain of the exact wording or policy number of a CSULB policy on "authorized vendors." Generally, CSULB follows CSU system procurement rules, under which only staff with delegated purchasing authority, usually in Procurement Services, can commit university funds or sign agreements with vendors. A vendor typically has to be set up as an approved supplier in the university's financial system, which usually requires tax documentation such as a W-9 or a California Payee Data Record, before purchase orders or payments can be issued. Employees who make purchases or sign contracts without that authority may be held personally responsible for the obligation. For the specific requirements, check with CSULB Procurement Services or the university's official policy website.

I can't recall the exact wording of the "Controlled Games" section of CSULB's Fund Guidelines, so I can only describe what such provisions generally cover. In California, "controlled games" usually refers to gambling-type activities such as raffles, casino or poker nights, and other games of chance. University fund guidelines typically restrict or prohibit using university or auxiliary funds to sponsor them, or to hold them as fundraisers, unless they meet state law. Raffles, for example, are generally allowed only for eligible nonprofits registered with the California Attorney General under Penal Code section 320.5, and they must follow its rules on proceeds and prizes. For the exact CSULB requirements, check the current Fund Guidelines document or ask the office that administers it, such as Associated Students, the CSULB Foundation, or University Accounting.

At CSULB, hazard assessment is mainly addressed through the campus Injury and Illness Prevention Program (IIPP) and Personal Protective Equipment (PPE) program, administered by Environmental Health and Safety (EH&S), which implement Cal/OSHA requirements. Under Title 8, California Code of Regulations, Section 3380, supervisors must assess their work areas for hazards that require PPE, select appropriate equipment, train employees in its use, and document the assessment in a written certification. The IIPP (Cal/OSHA Title 8, Section 3203) also requires periodic inspections to identify and correct unsafe conditions, with reassessments when new processes, equipment, or hazards are introduced. For the exact current procedures and forms, check with CSULB EH&S, since I can't confirm the specifics of the campus documents.

I can't recall the exact wording or policy number, so please treat this as a general outline. CSULB's rules on delegating signature authority generally allow the official who granted a delegation, typically the President or the appropriate Vice President, to revoke or change it at any time, and revocation should be documented in writing. A delegation also usually ends automatically when the delegate leaves the position or the delegating official's own authority changes, because the authority belongs to the position rather than the individual. For the exact language and any notice requirements, check CSULB's current delegation of authority policy or ask Financial Management or Contract Services.

I can't recall the exact wording or policy number of CSULB's Policy on Student Media, so I can only describe how such provisions typically work. Student media policies at public California universities generally allow student editors broad freedom under the First Amendment and California Education Code Section 66301 but exclude material that is legally obscene. "Obscene" in this context is a narrow legal category, usually defined by the U.S. Supreme Court's *Miller v. California* test and California Penal Code Section 311: material that, taken as a whole, appeals to a prurient interest in sex, depicts sexual conduct in a patently offensive way, and lacks serious literary, artistic, political, or scientific value. Content that is merely vulgar, profane, sexually frank, or offensive to some readers is generally still protected, so this kind of clause doesn't let the university censor content simply because it's distasteful. For the exact language, check the policy on CSULB's website or ask the Student Media office or the Office of Academic Senate.

As I understand it, the CSULB policy on external evaluation of research, scholarly, and creative activities (RSCA) treats the external evaluator's report as a supplement to, not a replacement for, the RTP review. The report assesses the quality and significance of the candidate's RSCA within the discipline. It is not meant to recommend whether the candidate should be retained, tenured, or promoted. Once received, the report is placed in the candidate's dossier (the Working Personnel Action File), and the candidate gets a copy and can submit a written response or rebuttal within the usual timeframe. I'm not certain of the policy number or the finer procedural details, such as how evaluators are selected or how confidentiality is handled, so check the current policy on the CSULB Academic Senate website.

I can't quote the exact wording of the fiscal reporting provision in CSU Executive Order 890, "Administration of Grants and Contracts," which applies to CSULB as a CSU campus. My general understanding is that it requires the sponsored program administrator, whether the campus or an auxiliary such as the CSULB Research Foundation, to ensure that fiscal reports to sponsors are accurate, complete, timely, and consistent with the sponsor's terms and conditions. It also ties those reports to the official accounting records and to applicable federal, state, and CSU requirements, such as federal cost principles and audit standards. For the precise language, check the full text of EO 890 on the CSU Chancellor's Office policy site or ask CSULB's Office of Research and Sponsored Programs.

At CSULB, the restoration of a respondent's reputation is addressed in the university's research misconduct policy, which follows federal Public Health Service requirements (42 CFR Part 93). If an allegation is not substantiated, the university makes reasonable, diligent efforts to restore the respondent's reputation, as appropriate and usually in consultation with the respondent. Such efforts may include notifying people who knew about the allegation or were involved in the inquiry or investigation that it was not substantiated, publicizing the final outcome where the allegation had been publicized, and removing references to the matter from the respondent's personnel file. I'm not certain of the exact policy number or current wording, so check the official text with CSULB's Office of Research and Sponsored Programs or the Academic Senate policy listings.
